newsitem.title: GUAM: Grim work resumes at Guam plane crash site.
newsitem.headline: Grim work resumes at Guam plane crash site.

text.p: U.S. recovery teams and relatives of the dead on Friday resumed the grim task of retrieving and identifying bodies from the Korean Air Lines (KAL) jet which ploughed into a jungle as it tried to land at Guam's airport.
"The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation as well as the search for bodies began first thing this morning," a Guam government spokesman said.
More than 100 bodies were yet to be pulled out from the wreck of the KAL jumbo jet which crashed into low-lying hills just three miles (five km) from the airport early on Wednesday.

The U.S. military, initially in charge of the rescue and recovery effort at the wreck of the Boeing 747, had suspended its operations on Thursday to wait for the NTSB experts to take over the job and start the investigation.
NTSB team leader George Black said on Thursday it was too early to speculate on the cause of the crash.
In Washington, NTSB officials said that the "black box" voice and data recorders were in surprisingly good shape and should provide a great deal of information on what caused the crash.

"Both are in excellent shape, the tapes are in good shape. There is useful data from both the black boxes," Dr Vernon Ellingstad, director of research and engineering at the National Transportation Safety Board, told reporters.
Flight 801 was carrying 254 people, mostly South Korean vacationers, from Seoul to Guam. It crashed while attempting to land at the airport in a heavy downpour.

Twenty-seven people survived the crash. One, 11-year old Rika Matsuda from Japan, had only light injuries, eight were transferred to hospitals in Seoul on Thursday and more were to be evacuated to South Korean hospitals.

"The next stage is to medi-vac all patients to South Korea," said hospital administrator Tyrone Taitano at the Guam Memorial Hospital. His hospital had 12 crash survivors and the rest were at the Guam Navy Hospital.
So far, U.S. military search teams have recovered the bodies of about 69 people and anguished members of Korean families were still waiting for the final word on their loved ones.
U.S. military officials said the recovered bodies were in bad condition and that this had precluded an accurate body count.
A team of forensic experts were on their way from Los Angeles to help with the identification process, Guam government officials said.
